title: Whistleblower channels, protections and reprisal
notes: The Inspector General route Grusch took, the whistleblower bills and the reprisal record.

lead.text: On 25 May 2022 Charles McCullough III, the first Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, filed David Grusch's urgent-concern complaint with that office, which found it credible and urgent in July 2022. What followed was a reprisal complaint, House whistleblower bills that never left referral, and a congressional letter on reprisal that the Department had not answered by September 2025.

summary.text: Two inspectors general are involved: the Intelligence Community Inspector General, who received Grusch's complaint and later briefed House members, and the Defense Department's Inspector General, whose 2023 evaluation of the Department's UAP handling is classified except for a summary.

In the House, Tim Burchett's UAP Whistleblower Protection Act was filed in 2024 and again in 2025, and the reprisal case against Grusch entered the record through Rep. Eli Crane's letter at the September 2025 hearing.
The members pressing these channels hold no statutory entitlement to see waived special access programmes, and a caucus confers none.

record.text: Grusch's PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint was filed with the ICIG on 25 May 2022 by his counsel McCullough, a senior partner at Compass Rose Legal Group, and found credible and urgent in July 2022, which obliges transmission to the congressional intelligence committees. Grusch testified that he became a whistleblower through that filing.

Grusch described the complaint's subject under oath as material acquisition and exploitation activity, and the baselining of UAP without sharing it with the intelligence professionals who brief pilots.

Thomas Monheim held the Inspector General's office when the finding was made, and his office briefed House Oversight members in closed session in January 2024; members publicly reported learning nothing new.

The Defense Department Inspector General's evaluation DODIG-2023-109, dated 15 August 2023, is classified (the office is now led by Platte B. Moring III); its 16-page unclassified summary, released in January 2024, found that the Department had no overarching UAP policy and so lacked assurance that UAP threats to national security and flight safety had been identified and mitigated.

The summary also found no comprehensive UAP response plan, no formal requirement that components report UAP incidents to AARO, differing service reporting systems, and geographic combatant commanders largely excluded from policy development. It made eleven recommendations; the first, a department-wide UAP policy, was left resolved but open.

Burchett's H.R. 10111 was introduced on 12 November 2024 with Mace, Luna and Burlison as cosponsors, and his H.R. 5060 on 29 August 2025 with Luna and Crane; both were referred to Oversight and additionally to the Intelligence and Armed Services committees, and neither has advanced beyond referral.
Burlison said on the record that the bill is language that would protect whistleblowers from reprisal and that it is blocked again and again, often by staff rather than elected officials.

Crane's letter to the Defense Department of 24 July 2025 states that Grusch suffered reprisal including removal of his clearance, denial of promotion and loss of medical retirement. Crane entered it into the 9 September 2025 hearing record saying he was still waiting for a reply, and Luna said the Task Force would follow up.

Before the 2023 hearing members were denied a classified briefing in a SCIF because of the steps needed to give Grusch temporary clearance, and Andy Ogles offered to invoke the Holman Rule against any personnel, programme or agency that denied Congress access to him.
Nancy Mace sits on House Armed Services but holds neither the chair nor the ranking seat, so she receives nothing under 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2).

claimed.text: Grusch testified that he suffered retaliation for his disclosures. His reprisal complaint alleges that his identity and his communications with the DoD Inspector General were disclosed to parties outside the Inspector General's office, and The Debrief records an earlier protected disclosure to the DoD Inspector General in July 2021.
Grusch testified that there was no smooth process for the ICIG to give his disclosure to the House and Senate Armed Services committees despite its Title 10 equities.

Eric Davis, on American Alchemy in December 2024, described three separate acts against Grusch between his complaint and his testimony: harassment by someone at the NRO, physical harassment at home and in his vehicles by people unknown, and a leak of a PTSD episode from his medical files. The board keeps the three apart because they have different actors.

After the January 2024 ICIG briefing Burchett said about sixteen members had attended, rated it four out of ten and called it very compartmentalized; Ogles said he asked specific questions and could not get specific answers and described a concerted effort to conceal.

Dylan Borland testified that his career was deliberately obstructed for more than a decade and that many who come forward feel discarded; he says he filed complaints with AARO in March 2023 and the ICIG in August 2023, and later said AARO transmitted an uncorrected memorandum of his interview to ODNI.

DefenseScoop reported that lawmakers took up H.R. 5060 before the September 2025 hearing because existing channels were judged inadequate for UAP witnesses; the board infers that a separate channel is sought because AARO's mechanism is not a safe destination, citing AARO's own count of 255 of 262 contacts declared out of scope.

contested.text: The ICIG found the complaint credible and urgent in 2022, while AARO found no verifiable information in 2023 and no firsthand knowledge among its interviewees in 2024; the board records the two executive-branch findings as never reconciled.
AARO's memorandum documents its approaches to Grusch and a missed November 2023 appointment and makes the non-appearance the centre of its impeachment; Grusch has cited legal and security exposure.

The board infers that a credible-and-urgent finding that legally went to the intelligence committees, followed eighteen months later by a briefing members found empty, was absorbed without producing disclosure.

On the board's reading, a classified evaluation whose scope cannot be checked works in the public record as assurance rather than evidence, and components not required to report to AARO make its holdings a self-selected sample.
The records date the ICIG briefing differently, to 12 January and to 13 January 2024.

questions: Did the Defense Department ever answer Crane's July 2025 letter, and on what date and under what authority was Grusch's clearance removed?
Did the ICIG investigate the underlying allegations, or only the reprisal claim, and how was the reprisal complaint resolved?
Did the substance of Grusch's complaint ever reach the Armed Services committees that oversee the programmes it concerns?
Will the classified DODIG-2023-109 report be released, and has its first recommendation been closed?
Is there any Inspector General or MSPB record of the retaliation Borland describes?
Why have both whistleblower protection bills stayed in referral, and who blocks them?
